cards.note: The 1933 ICI record is well sourced, but origin is not first known: a 1898 accidental preparation of polymethylene by Hans von Pechmann is reported in secondary sources I could not open, so origin is left as unknown. Dates of the 1933 setup differ between sources (24 March in the Science Museum record).
cards.name: Polyethylene at ICI Winnington, Cheshire
cards.summary: A waxy solid made by accident at ICI Winnington in 1933 was reproduced in 1935 and went into full-scale production in 1939.
cards.description: In 1933 ICI chemists Reginald Gibson and Eric Fawcett heated ethylene with benzaldehyde at high pressure and obtained a waxy solid, polyethylene, at Winnington near Northwich. In December 1935 Edmond Williams, Michael Perrin and John Paton reproduced it from ethylene alone, and the first full-scale plant began production on 1 September 1939. Polyethylene then insulated British airborne radar cables during the Second World War.
cards.origin_note: The sources show ICI found the material by accident in 1933 but do not say whether the team knew of an earlier synthesis; an 1898 preparation by Hans von Pechmann is reported elsewhere and could not be checked here.

impact.note: Kept the curator's scores: the sources show wide use in cables, bags and bottles, but not a reorganisation of an activity beyond that.

cards.why: ICI's Bernard Habgood recognised that polyethylene could replace gutta-percha for submarine cable insulation, which gave the impetus to commercial production.

events.statement: A waxy solid formed during high-pressure experiments at ICI Winnington in 1933 was first seen by Gibson and Fawcett.
events.quote: The waxy solid had been formed during high-pressure experiments conducted in 1933 by ICI scientists Reginald Gibson and Eric Fawcett.

events.label: December 1935
events.statement: In December 1935 Williams, Perrin and Paton repeated the high-pressure reaction with ethylene alone and obtained a white polymer powder.
events.quote: In December that year, Williams and colleagues Michael Perrin and John Paton reinvestigated the experiments of Gibson and Fawcett using ethylene alone.

events.label: 1 September 1939
events.statement: ICI's first full-scale polyethylene plant, of 100 tonnes a year, went into production on 1 September 1939.
events.quote: The first full-scale PE plant, with a 100 tonne/year capacity, went into production on September 1, 1939, the day Germany invaded Poland

events.label: Second World War
events.statement: During the Second World War polyethylene was used to insulate airborne radar equipment, reducing its weight.
events.quote: PE’s electrical insulation properties enabled the British forces to reduce the weight of radar equipment and allowed them to place radars inside fighter planes.

sources.title: Polyethylene: discovered by accident 75 years ago

open_questions: Whether Hans von Pechmann's 1898 accidental preparation (polymethylene from diazomethane) should be its own record, and whether ICI's 1933 work was independent of it. Needs a fetchable primary or review source.
The exact day of the 1933 experiment: the Science Museum record gives Friday 24 March 1933 and some other sources give 27 March.
The 1953 low-pressure routes (Ziegler; Hogan and Banks at Phillips) are not in this card and should be a separate record linked to polypropylene or HDPE.

cards.name: Barkcloth (tapa) in the Pacific Islands
cards.summary: Austronesian voyagers carried paper mulberry and the beater into Remote Oceania, where barkcloth became the main cloth and ceremonial wrapping.
cards.description: Barkcloth made by beating the inner bark of paper mulberry, known as tapa, was carried by Austronesian-speaking colonists into Remote Oceania. Lapita culture reached Tonga and Samoa by about 2900 BP, and the most common Pacific paper mulberry has a Taiwanese origin. Tapa was used for clothing, ceremonial artefacts and gift exchange, and its production declined with European woven cloth.
cards.origin_note: Genetic evidence traces the dominant Pacific paper mulberry to Taiwan, and the early Pacific barkcloth tradition is linked to Austronesian cultures, so the practice was transmitted rather than reinvented.

impact.note: Kept the curator's scores: barkcloth was central to Pacific life across many islands, but the sources describe it within one region and do not show later work resting on it.

events.label: c. 6050 BCE
events.statement: The earliest stone barkcloth beater known from the region is from Guangxi in southern China, dated to around 8000 BP, about 6050 BCE.
events.quote: where the earliest stone barkcloth beater has been found in Guangxi, Southern China, and dates to around 8000 BP

events.label: by about 950 BCE
events.statement: Lapita culture reached Tonga and Samoa by about 2900 BP, and the most common Pacific paper mulberry, most likely brought by the early colonists, has a Taiwanese origin.
events.quote: reaching Tonga and Samoa, on the edge of the Polynesian Triangle by about 2900 BP

sources.title: Tracking Austronesian expansion into the Pacific via the paper mulberry plant
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

sources.title: A holistic picture of Austronesian migrations revealed by phylogeography of Pacific paper mulberry
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

open_questions: The Dingmo beater paper (Quaternary International, 2014) could not be opened; the date given here comes from the PNAS commentary, which is a secondary citation.
Whether the Pacific tapa beaters were carried by the same colonists as the paper mulberry, as the Chang et al. data suggest, needs a dated Pacific beater or plant record.
Barkcloth in Central Africa and bark beating in Mesoamerica are independent per the curator and were not checked here.

cards.lead: Engineered paved road network of Rome
cards.note: The Via Appia (312 BCE) is well sourced as the start of a major Roman road, but the sources do not say the road was independent of Etruscan or Persian roads, so origin is unknown. Britannica also dates the start of Roman road-making to 334 BCE, earlier than the lead's 312 BCE.
cards.name: Roman state road network
cards.summary: Rome built a system of engineered military roads radiating from the capital, beginning with the Appian Way in 312 BCE.
cards.description: The Romans began road-making in 334 BCE, according to Britannica, and by the peak of the empire had built nearly 53,000 miles of road linking the capital with its frontiers. The Appian Way, begun in 312 BCE, ran south from Rome to Capua and then to Brundisium. Twenty-nine great military roads radiated from Rome.
cards.origin_note: The sources give the Roman dates but do not say whether Roman road building was independent of Etruscan or Persian roads, so the evidence does not settle it.

impact.note: Kept the curator's scores: the network served much of the empire for centuries, and the sources do not show later work built directly on it.

events.label: 334 BCE
events.statement: Britannica states that the Romans began their road-making task in 334 BCE.
events.quote: The Romans began their road-making task in 334 bce and by the peak of the empire had built nearly 53,000 miles of road connecting their capital with the frontiers of their far-flung empire.

events.label: 312 BCE
events.statement: The Appian Way was begun in 312 BCE and followed the coast south to Capua in Campania.
events.quote: Begun in 312 bce, this road eventually followed the Mediterranean coast south to Capua

open_questions: Whether the 334 BCE date for the start of Roman road-making refers to a specific road, and what it is; the Appian Way is the first road the sources date.
Whether Roman road building was independent of Etruscan roads and of the Persian royal roads; the Persian system and the Qin and Han highways each merit a record.
The network's peak extent (about 53,000 miles per Britannica) is undated, so it is not an event here.

cards.lead: Iron-chain suspension bridges in southwest China and the Himalaya
cards.note: Searched for the earliest iron-chain bridge in China and for Thangtong Gyalpo's bridges. The 1430 Chushul Chakzam date appears in the sources I could reach only through Wikipedia, which I cannot cite; Manfred Gerner's monograph, which Wikipedia cites for it, was not reachable from the fetcher. The Chinese claims (Tang-era or c. 600 CE iron chains, the 1475 Jihong bridge) were found only on secondary pages, so no earliest date for iron chains could be cited.

cards.lead: Controlled-access motorways in Italy and Germany
cards.note: The lead's 'first known' motorway is contested. The AVUS in Berlin was opened to general motor traffic in 1921, three years before the Milan to the lakes road, and the Milan road is only called the world's first motorway by its operator. Whether any of these had no crossings at grade is not settled by the sources opened, so origin is unknown and the lead's 1924 date is not the first known.
cards.name: Early motor-only roads: AVUS, Milan-Lakes and Cologne-Bonn
cards.summary: Germany and Italy opened motor-only roads between 1921 and 1932, the earliest being the AVUS in Berlin.
cards.description: The AVUS in Berlin was opened for races on 24 and 25 September 1921 and cleared for general motor traffic on 1 October 1921. The inaugural section of the Milan to the lakes road between Lainate and Gallarate was opened on 21 September 1924. The Cologne to Bonn road, begun in 1929, was completed on 6 August 1932 as Germany's first motorway project.
cards.origin_note: The sources date three separate motor-only roads and do not show that any one drew on another, but they do not establish independence either.

impact.note: Lowered reach from the curator's 3: the sources show national road building in Germany and Italy and no spread beyond them that this record can cite.

events.label: 1 October 1921
events.statement: The AVUS in Berlin was cleared for general motor traffic on 1 October 1921, after its opening races, and charged a toll.
events.quote: After the opening races at the end of September the AVUS was cleared for general motor traffic on 1 st October 1921.
events.locator: Article text, section on the first years

events.label: 21 September 1924
events.statement: The inaugural section of the Milan to the lakes road, between Lainate and Gallarate, was inaugurated on 21 September 1924 with King Victor Emmanuel III present.
events.quote: On 21 September 1924, Victor Emmanuel III, on board his Lancia Trikappa, travelled the few kilometres between Lainate and Gallarate

events.label: 6 August 1932
events.statement: The Cologne to Bonn road, begun in 1929, was completed on 6 August 1932 as Germany's first motorway project.
events.quote: die als erstes Autobahnprojekt Deutschlands am 6. August 1932 vollendet wurde

sources.title: The oldest and most complex network in Europe

open_questions: Whether the AVUS, the Milan to the lakes road and the Cologne to Bonn road had no crossings at grade and entry only at junctions, which is the controlled-access test. The sources opened do not say.
The Long Island Motor Parkway (1908) and American parkways were earlier car-only roads, named by the curator; they were not checked here.
The Milan road is called the world's first motorway by its operator; that claim needs an independent source before it is repeated.

cards.lead: Organised night-soil collection in the cities of Song China
cards.note: The sources place the practice in Zhejiang: a Southern Song text of about 1212 describes collection and storage in Quzhou and Wuzhou, and Wu Zimu's Dreams of Liang describes paid, area-based collectors in Hangzhou, but that text is not dated in the source. The earliest dated record is therefore c. 1212, not 1150, and origin is unknown rather than first known.
cards.name: Night-soil collection in Song Zhejiang
cards.summary: Households in Song-dynasty Zhejiang collected and stored night soil for fertiliser, and Hangzhou had collectors with fixed clienteles.
cards.description: Cheng Mi, writing about 1212, described the people of Quzhou and Wuzhou collecting and storing night soil in large heaps, which he credited with fertile soil and good rice. Wu Zimu's Dreams of Liang describes Hangzhou's designated night soil collectors, the qing jiaotou, each with a fixed clientele that other collectors did not encroach on. The Hangzhou description is not dated in the source opened.
cards.origin_note: The sources show the practice in Song Zhejiang but do not show who began it or whether it was derived from earlier practice elsewhere, so origin is not settled.

impact.note: Lowered reach from the curator's 2: the sources describe the practice in one region of Zhejiang. Generativity kept at 0 because no later line of work is cited here.

cards.why: Hangzhou had a large, dense population whose households lacked pit latrines and relied on chamber pots, so a daily collection was needed.

events.label: c. 1212
events.statement: Cheng Mi, writing about 1212, described households in Quzhou and Wuzhou collecting and storing night soil in large heaps.
events.quote: I have often seen the people of Quzhou and Wuzhou collecting and storing night soil, with every household accumulating it in great mounds
events.locator: Section on night soil fertilizer and the Song farming economy, quoting Cheng Mi (ca. 1212)

sources.title: Night soil fertilizer use and parasitic infections in ancient China: a preliminary study of agricultural practices, economic factors and disease ecology in the Song dynasty

open_questions: A dated source for the Hangzhou collectors described in Wu Zimu's Dreams of Liang (Mengliang lu). The modern article quotes the text without giving the date of the passage.

Whether the Hangzhou collectors held contracts or licences, as the lead's 'waste reuse contract' concept implies; the sources opened describe fixed clienteles and official management, not written contracts.
Earlier evidence for night-soil fertiliser and collection, and Edo Japan's commercial night-soil trade, which may merit a derived record; neither was checked here.
